title: Nauru Achieves Independence from Australian Trusteeship
description: On 31 January 1968 Nauru gained independence under Founding President Hammer DeRoburt, ending Australian-administered trusteeship. The 21-square-kilometre island became the world's smallest republic by area.

title: Nauru Phosphate Corporation Acquires Mining Operations
description: The Nauru Phosphate Corporation took over operations from the British Phosphate Commissioners, channelling royalties directly to the Nauruan government. Nauru briefly became one of the world's wealthiest nations on a per-capita basis.

title: Bernard Dowiyogo Becomes President
description: Bernard Dowiyogo defeated Hammer DeRoburt to become president for the first of seven separate terms, opening an era of unstable executive politics. The Nauruan parliament's small size made motions of no-confidence unusually frequent.

title: Nauru Sues Australia at the International Court of Justice
description: Nauru initiated proceedings against Australia at the ICJ over pre-independence phosphate damage to the island's interior. The case settled out of court in 1993 with a substantial compensation package.

title: Settlement With Australia Over Phosphate Damage
description: Australia agreed to a roughly AUD 107 million settlement plus rehabilitation contributions in exchange for Nauru ending its ICJ case. The funds went into the Nauru Rehabilitation Trust.

title: Trust Fund Investment Failures Surface
description: Reports emerged that the Nauru Phosphate Royalties Trust had suffered enormous losses on offshore property and venture investments, including a London musical and Australian hotels. The losses pushed the country toward eventual insolvency.

title: Nauru Admitted to the United Nations
description: Nauru joined the United Nations on 14 September 1999 alongside Kiribati and Tonga. UN membership came three decades after independence and gave the microstate its first formal global voice.

title: Offshore Banking Sector Closed Under FATF Pressure
description: Under FATF blacklisting and US Treasury pressure, Nauru's offshore banking sector was wound down after exposure as a major Russian money-laundering channel. The closure ended a brief but reputationally damaging financial-services chapter.

title: Pacific Solution Detention Centre Opens at Topside
description: Nauru agreed in September 2001 to host the Australian-funded offshore detention centre for asylum seekers under the 'Pacific Solution', following the Tampa incident. The facility provided crucial budget support to a near-bankrupt government.

title: Multiple Presidents in Single Year
description: Nauru cycled through several presidents in 2003 amid the deepest fiscal crisis since independence and the death of Bernard Dowiyogo in office in March. Parliamentary instability briefly left the country with no functioning executive at all.

title: Nauru Defaults on Sovereign Debts
description: Creditors seized Nauruan-owned property in Australia and elsewhere as the government defaulted on bond and bank obligations. The defaults marked the formal end of the post-independence phosphate-funded prosperity model.

title: State of Emergency Over Fiscal Collapse
description: Acting President Ludwig Scotty declared a state of emergency in 2004 to push through austerity measures and tax reforms. Government salaries had gone unpaid for months and basic services were near collapse.

title: Diplomatic Switch from Beijing to Taipei
description: Nauru re-recognised the Republic of China (Taiwan) in May 2005 after an earlier 2002 switch to Beijing. The move restored Taiwanese aid and triggered a Chinese diplomatic withdrawal.

title: Pacific Solution Detention Centre Initially Closed
description: The Australian Labor government formally closed the Nauru detention centre in early 2008 after the change of government in Canberra. Nauru lost a major source of budget support and Australian aid spiked to compensate.

title: Constitutional Reform Referendum Fails
description: A referendum on direct election of the president and other constitutional changes failed to reach the supermajority threshold in February 2010. The defeat preserved the unstable parliamentary executive model.

title: Australian Detention Centre Reopens
description: The Australian Gillard government reopened the Nauru regional processing centre in September 2012 under bipartisan support. The reopened facility once again became central to Australian asylum policy and to Nauruan public finances.

title: Detention Centre Riot and Fires
description: Asylum seekers detained at the Nauru centre staged a major protest in July 2013 that escalated into rioting and arson, destroying much of the facility. The incident attracted international human rights scrutiny of the offshore-processing model.

title: Magistrate and Chief Justice Expelled
description: President Baron Waqa's government deported the resident Australian magistrate and revoked the Chief Justice's visa in 2014, drawing accusations of an attack on judicial independence. The episode triggered a regional rule-of-law reckoning.

title: Opposition MPs Suspended and Charged
description: Five opposition members of parliament were suspended in 2014 and faced criminal charges in 2015 in the so-called 'Nauru 19' case. Civil society groups described the prosecutions as politically motivated suppression of dissent.

title: Pacific Islands Forum Hosted in Yaren
description: Nauru hosted the Pacific Islands Forum leaders' meeting in September 2018, drawing Chinese protests over Taiwan's invitation and over the visa treatment of Chinese officials. The summit underscored Nauru's outsized geopolitical leverage.

title: Lionel Aingimea Elected President
description: Lionel Aingimea was elected by parliament in August 2019, succeeding Baron Waqa. The new administration committed to a less confrontational tone with the judiciary and civil society.

title: COVID-19 Border Closure
description: Nauru closed its borders in early 2020 and remained one of the world's last COVID-free jurisdictions for nearly two years. Asylum seekers and refugee residents continued to be a major government and donor concern through the pandemic.

title: Russ Kun Elected President
description: Russ Kun was elected president by parliament in September 2022 after the general election. His government reaffirmed Taiwan recognition and sought new fiscal partnerships.

title: David Adeang Elected President
description: Long-serving cabinet minister David Adeang was elected president in October 2023 after a parliamentary realignment. His incoming government immediately re-examined Nauru's diplomatic alignment with Taipei.

title: Diplomatic Switch from Taipei to Beijing
description: President Adeang's government severed ties with Taiwan and re-recognised the People's Republic of China on 15 January 2024, days after Taiwan's presidential election. The switch unlocked Chinese aid pledges and ended a near 20-year alignment with Taipei.

title: Australia and Nauru Sign Strategic Treaty
description: Nauru and Australia signed a bilateral treaty in late 2024 deepening defence, banking and migration cooperation, partly to counter Chinese diplomatic gains. The treaty included a security veto clause similar to the Australia-Tuvalu Falepili Union.

title: Deep-Sea Mining Sponsorship Continues
description: Nauru continued to sponsor The Metals Company's bid for deep-sea polymetallic nodule mining licences in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, drawing both potential revenue hopes and criticism from neighbouring Pacific states. The International Seabed Authority continued debating the regulatory framework.

title: Climate Vulnerability and Phosphate Exhaustion
description: Continued sea-level pressure on coastal infrastructure and the near-exhaustion of remaining secondary phosphate reserves left Nauru reliant on detention-centre fees, fishing revenue and donor flows. The government formally explored 'climate visa' programmes for citizens.

title: Citizenship-by-Investment Scheme Launched
description: Nauru launched a climate-funded golden passport programme in 2025, intending to raise revenue for adaptation projects through the sale of citizenship to wealthy foreigners. The scheme drew international concern over due-diligence standards.
